name: Systemic EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma of childhood
aliases: systemic EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma of childhood
systemic EBV-positive T-cell lymphoproliferative disease of childhood
EBV-associated haemophagocytic T-cell lymphoma of children

clinicalPearls: A rare, fulminant clonal T-cell proliferation of children and young adults that follows acute or chronic active Epstein-Barr virus infection
It is classified as a lymphoid neoplasm because of the clonal, aggressive nature of the process despite its viral driver
Presents with a rapidly progressive systemic illness including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, liver dysfunction and cytopenias
Almost always complicated by haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, which dominates the acute clinical picture
The neoplastic cells are Epstein-Barr virus-positive (EBER-positive) cytotoxic T cells, usually CD8-positive, and are clonal by T-cell receptor analysis
It is far more common in East Asian and Latin American populations, indicating a genetic predisposition to abnormal Epstein-Barr virus handling
Requires urgent immunochemotherapy directed at both the lymphoma and the haemophagocytic syndrome, with allogeneic HSCT offering the main chance of cure
reference.pathophysiology: Systemic EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma of childhood develops when Epstein-Barr virus infects T cells and, against a background of genetically impaired antiviral immunity, drives a clonal and rapidly proliferating population of virus-infected cytotoxic T lymphocytes. The infected clone and the surrounding immune response release large quantities of inflammatory cytokines, activating macrophages and precipitating haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with its attendant cytopenias, coagulopathy and multi-organ dysfunction. The neoplastic cells infiltrate the liver, spleen, marrow and lymphoid tissue, and the combination of clonal proliferation and cytokine-driven hyperinflammation produces the characteristically fulminant course that can progress to multi-organ failure within days to weeks.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic active Epstein-Barr virus infection of T/NK-cell type
Acute leukaemia or other aggressive systemic lymphoma in a child
additionalInvestigations: Epstein-Barr virus studies including EBER in situ hybridisation on tissue and viral load in blood
Immunophenotyping showing EBV-positive cytotoxic T cells, usually CD8-positive
Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis workup including ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, soluble interleukin-2 receptor and bone marrow examination
Liver function and coagulation studies given frequent hepatic involvement
Imaging to assess hepatosplenomegaly and disease extent
redFlags: Fulminant haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with multi-organ dysfunction
Rapidly worsening liver failure and coagulopathy
Severe cytopenias with bleeding or overwhelming infection
reference.prognosis: The disorder is highly aggressive and frequently fatal within a short period, often from fulminant haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and multi-organ failure; survival is poor without prompt intensive therapy, and allogeneic HSCT offers the main prospect of long-term cure in those who respond.
pitfalls: Mistaking the illness for a self-limiting viral infection or purely reactive haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and delaying treatment
Failing to demonstrate the clonal EBV-positive T-cell population
Underestimating the speed of clinical deterioration
Confusing it with chronic active Epstein-Barr virus infection, which has a different course
Not recognising the higher incidence and predisposition in East Asian and Latin American children
references: British Society for Haematology and international guidance on EBV-associated lymphoproliferative disorders
management: This is a rare, rapidly progressive systemic disease almost always complicated by hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), so treatment must start urgently once diagnosed
Surgery has no curative role beyond diagnostic biopsy, and radiotherapy is not part of standard management since the disease is systemic rather than localized

First priority is controlling the hyperinflammatory HLH component using HLH directed immunochemotherapy, combining an etoposide based cytotoxic agent, corticosteroids, and a calcineurin inhibitor such as ciclosporin

In parallel with HLH directed therapy, lymphoma directed combination chemotherapy targets the clonal EBV positive cytotoxic T-cell population itself, since HLH therapy alone does not eliminate the malignant clone

Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant is the definitive step regarded as the main route to durable cure once disease control is achieved, since chemotherapy alone is not curative in most reported experience
Transplant referral should happen early and ideally in parallel with induction rather than only after chemotherapy completion, given the pace of the disease
No established standard salvage regimen exists for relapsed, refractory, or transplant ineligible disease in the literature reviewed
Intensive supportive care in a critical care setting is core to management, including correction of coagulopathy and cytopenias and support for hepatic and hemodynamic compromise
Blood product support and infection prophylaxis are needed through periods of profound cytopenia and immunosuppression from both disease and treatment

Monitor HLH markers including ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor along with blood counts, liver function, and coagulation studies to track response and detect organ deterioration early
Monitor EBV viral load and, where available, T-cell clonality and EBER status to track the underlying lymphoproliferative clone
Closely track transplant candidacy and timing, since delay while awaiting a donor or organ recovery can allow disease progression
Refer immediately to a specialist pediatric hemato-oncology center with transplant capability at diagnosis, given the disease's speed and the central role of allogeneic transplant
Offer family counseling and evaluation for an underlying genetic predisposition to abnormal EBV handling, particularly given higher incidence in East Asian and Latin American populations
